sections.title: VTE prevention & postoperative recovery
bullets: Assess cancer, prior VTE, obesity, immobility and bleeding risk. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with surgical hemostasis, renal function, drug interactions and neuraxial placement/removal; surgery timing does not override anticoagulant safety intervals.

For cancer laparotomy, the 2026 ERAS update recommends combined mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis and 28-day postoperative prophylaxis with LMWH or an appropriate DOAC. Drug choice requires an individualized bleeding, renal-function, interaction and adherence assessment; this is not a universal drug or dose prescription.

Do not automatically extend that 28-day regimen to minimally invasive surgery or minor benign procedures. The 2026 guideline favors mechanical prophylaxis for MIS and considers pharmacologic prophylaxis for high-risk patients, including a high Caprini score; follow the applicable oncology risk assessment.

The ERAS recommendation to initiate surgical prophylaxis preoperatively within two hours of incision is not permission to give LMWH immediately before neuraxial placement. ASRA recommends at least 12 hours after low-dose LMWH before needle placement; higher-dose regimens and renal impairment need their own assessment.

For twice-daily low-dose postoperative LMWH, ASRA requires the first dose the following day and at least 12 hours after needle/catheter placement, catheter removal before LMWH begins, and at least four hours from removal to LMWH. Use the full guideline for other regimens, traumatic placement and concurrent anticoagulants.

Support mobilization and oral nutrition within 24 hours when clinically appropriate. The ERAS regular-diet recommendation includes bowel resection, but instability, ileus, aspiration risk or specific reconstruction concerns require individualized surgical review, particularly after extensive exenteration.

sections.title: GLP-1 therapy: reconcile differing guidance
bullets: The 2026 gynecologic oncology ERAS table recommends holding daily GLP-1 therapy on the procedure day and weekly therapy for one week, with resumption on postoperative day one. This differs from the ASA-endorsed multisociety approach allowing continuation for most low-risk patients.

Do not translate either statement into an automatic patient instruction. Agree on a plan with anesthesia, the prescriber and surgery, considering dose escalation, gastrointestinal symptoms, other causes of delayed emptying, glycemic effects and the current institutional pathway.

For higher-risk patients the multisociety approach includes a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, adjustment of the anesthesia plan, and gastric ultrasound when appropriate expertise is available. Persistent concern may require delay of elective surgery; a medication hold or standard fasting interval does not prove an empty stomach.
Postoperative resumption also requires assessment of oral intake, nausea/vomiting, gastrointestinal function and the prescribing plan rather than an unconditional postoperative-day-one restart.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & optimization
bullets: Confirm indication, approach, pregnancy possibility and testing with consent under local policy. Review anemia, bleeding history, anticoagulants, obesity/OSA, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal function, prior pelvic operations and baseline neurologic symptoms.

Investigate and treat iron-deficiency anemia and nutritional deficits before elective major surgery when time permits. Urgent hemorrhage or source control should not wait for completion of an elective optimization pathway.

For elective gynecologic oncology surgery, identify and treat the cause of preoperative anemia, including iron deficiency. The 2026 ERAS update supports preoperative optimization; the route of iron replacement depends on severity and time available rather than a universal regimen.

Apply a procedure- and aspiration-risk-specific fasting plan. The ERAS oncology pathway permits clear fluids until two hours before anesthesia and supports preoperative carbohydrate drinks; this is not clearance for a patient with obstruction, delayed gastric emptying, active vomiting or emergency surgery. Assess vomiting, pain/opioids, reflux, obstruction, fasting and gestational stage individually. Severe postoperative leg pain, swelling or weakness can signal compartment syndrome even with palpable pulses; obtain urgent assessment rather than attributing it automatically to a block.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & fluid balance
bullets: Target euvolemia with reassessment of perfusion and measured losses; avoid both indiscriminate crystalloid loading and rigid restriction during bleeding. Distinguish vasodilation from hypovolemia or low cardiac output before choosing fluid, blood or vasoactive support.

Account for poor intake, bowel preparation, ascites drainage and irrigation absorption when relevant. Oliguria during pneumoperitoneum or pelvic manipulation is not by itself a mandate for repeated fluid boluses; inspect the catheter, hemodynamics and surgical context.

The 2026 ERAS guideline supports goal-directed fluid therapy for major gynecologic oncology surgery. Use an individualized hemodynamic assessment; it does not establish one universal monitor, fluid volume or vasoactive algorithm.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV prevention
bullets: Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with acetaminophen and an NSAID when renal function, bleeding risk and other contraindications permit. Local infiltration or an appropriate regional block may reduce incisional pain; blocks do not reliably eliminate visceral pelvic pain.

Assess PONV risk and use multimodal prophylaxis from different drug classes when indicated; consider propofol-based anesthesia and opioid reduction. Choose rescue antiemetics from a different class where possible and account for QT risk, sedation, urinary retention and other patient-specific effects.

For gynecologic oncology surgery, the 2026 ERAS recommendation is multimodal PONV prophylaxis with more than two antiemetic agents. Choose different classes with attention to contraindications and adverse effects rather than copying a fixed drug combination to every gynecologic procedure.

The updated oncology pathway supports multimodal analgesia, incisional local anesthetic or selected fascial-plane blocks, and intrathecal analgesia when appropriate. sections.title: VTE prevention & postoperative recovery
bullets: Assess cancer, prior VTE, obesity, immobility and bleeding risk. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with surgical hemostasis, renal function, drug interactions and neuraxial placement/removal; surgery timing does not override anticoagulant safety intervals.

For cancer laparotomy, the 2026 ERAS update recommends combined mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis and 28-day postoperative prophylaxis with LMWH or an appropriate DOAC. Drug choice requires an individualized bleeding, renal-function, interaction and adherence assessment; this is not a universal drug or dose prescription.

Do not automatically extend that 28-day regimen to minimally invasive surgery or minor benign procedures. The 2026 guideline favors mechanical prophylaxis for MIS and considers pharmacologic prophylaxis for high-risk patients, including a high Caprini score; follow the applicable oncology risk assessment.

The ERAS recommendation to initiate surgical prophylaxis preoperatively within two hours of incision is not permission to give LMWH immediately before neuraxial placement. For twice-daily low-dose postoperative LMWH, ASRA requires the first dose the following day and at least 12 hours after needle/catheter placement, catheter removal before LMWH begins, and at least four hours from removal to LMWH. Use the full guideline for other regimens, traumatic placement and concurrent anticoagulants.

Support mobilization and oral nutrition within 24 hours when clinically appropriate. sections.title: GLP-1 therapy: reconcile differing guidance

For higher-risk patients the multisociety approach includes a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, adjustment of the anesthesia plan, and gastric ultrasound when appropriate expertise is available. Persistent concern may require delay of elective surgery; a medication hold or standard fasting interval does not prove an empty stomach.
Postoperative resumption also requires assessment of oral intake, nausea/vomiting, gastrointestinal function and the prescribing plan rather than an unconditional postoperative-day-one restart.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: For most pregnant patients with cardiovascular disease, plan vaginal delivery with effective neuraxial analgesia; cesarean delivery is generally for obstetric indications or selected cardiac conditions.
Individualize monitoring and hemodynamic goals to the cardiac lesion and its severity.

Neuraxial anesthesia is often preferred when feasible, but technique and titration should reflect lesion severity, anticoagulation, and the risk of sympathectomy; general anesthesia is an option when neuraxial care is unsuitable or urgency requires it.
Recovery planning must account for postpartum hemodynamic and volume shifts, with monitoring intensity and location determined by the cardiac lesion and delivery course.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Favor planned vaginal delivery with effective neuraxial labor analgesia for most patients with cardiovascular disease; compared with cesarean delivery, it is associated with less blood loss, infection, and venous thromboembolism.

Cesarean delivery is generally for obstetric indications. The cardiac review identifies selected exceptions, including large expanding or dissecting aortic aneurysms, maternal warfarin anticoagulation, critical valvular stenosis, and severe decompensated pulmonary hypertension.

Choose neuraxial technique and onset deliberately. For selected severe lesions, gradual sympathectomy may be preferable to the faster hemodynamic changes associated with spinal anesthesia; technique remains dependent on lesion and clinical circumstances.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Arrange predelivery anesthetic assessment and multidisciplinary coordination with obstetrics and cardiology. Review the lesion, severity, cardiac history and testing, obstetric factors, anticipated anticoagulation, and resources needed for urgent intervention.

Use a recognized risk framework as an aid, not a substitute for clinical assessment. The mWHO classification spans a wide range of reported cardiovascular-event risk; pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe symptomatic aortic stenosis are examples of class IV lesions.

Plan delivery location according to anticipated expertise and rescue needs. Subspecialty cardiac care warrants a higher-level center; possible cardiac surgery or ECMO support favors a hospital with cardiac-surgery capability.
Assess anticoagulation before selecting neuraxial anesthesia. Coordinate timing and eligibility decisions with the multidisciplinary team, particularly for patients with mechanical valves.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Match staffing, location, vasoactive capability, and monitoring to lesion severity and anticipated intervention. Coordinate roles in advance where ECG monitoring or vasoactive/inotropic drug administration exceeds routine labor-unit capability.
Use left lateral positioning in labor when appropriate to relieve gravid-uterus compression; maintain uterine displacement for cesarean delivery.

Individualize monitoring. Intra-arterial pressure monitoring may help in selected high-risk lesions, especially when precise pressure management or emergency intervention is anticipated; it is not established here as mandatory for every cardiac condition.

During labor, consider continuous pulse oximetry and heart-rate monitoring; use ECG/telemetry when arrhythmia or ischemia risk warrants it. Invasive pulmonary monitoring is reserved for selected complex circumstances, not routine use.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial anesthesia is preferred for cesarean delivery whenever feasible, including in many patients with high-risk lesions. Consider general anesthesia when cardiopulmonary decompensation, anticoagulation, severe thrombocytopenia, refusal, or clinical urgency makes neuraxial anesthesia unsuitable.

If general anesthesia is chosen, account for the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation in the relevant lesion; the available cardiac review does not provide a general airway or induction protocol.

For pulmonary hypertension, avoid physiologic conditions that increase pulmonary vascular resistance, including hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, and high ventilation pressures when intubated; maintain attention to right-ventricular function.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Prevent abrupt reductions in systemic vascular resistance or pressure where fixed outflow obstruction or right-to-left shunting makes them poorly tolerated. For aortic stenosis, maintain afterload and avoid tachycardia; for right-to-left shunt, reduced systemic resistance can worsen shunting and hypoxia.
For pulmonary hypertension, avoid factors that increase pulmonary vascular resistance and optimize right-ventricular function.
Anticipate cardiovascular changes during labor and the postpartum period; patients with cardiovascular disease are at greatest risk of pulmonary edema during second-stage labor and postpartum.
Treat neuraxial-associated hypotension promptly, choosing vasopressor and fluid strategy in light of lesion physiology rather than applying a universal approach.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: New hypotension, hypoxia, tachycardia, or altered cardiac status warrants immediate assessment for lesion-related decompensation and obstetric causes. The cardiac review advises a low threshold for echocardiography, chest imaging, and ECG when heart disease is suspected.

For suspected pulmonary-hypertension or right-heart deterioration, avoid worsening hypoxia, hypercarbia, or acidosis and escalate promptly to the multidisciplinary team with relevant cardiopulmonary support available.
Prepare for arrhythmia and cardiac arrest through advance emergency planning and appropriate personnel/resources. This reference does not establish a cardiac-disease-specific resuscitation algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Maintain euvolemia, avoiding fluid overload in pulmonary hypertension or mitral stenosis. In aortic stenosis, augment preload judiciously because excess fluid can cause pulmonary edema; avoid routine fluid loading when pulmonary-edema risk is a concern.

The cardiac review notes that postpartum hemorrhage is more common in women with heart disease. Anticipate bleeding and coordinate uterotonic selection and administration with the cardiac lesion and obstetric team.

For cardiac disease, titrate oxytocin by infusion pump rather than giving a rapid bolus, because bolus administration can rapidly decrease systemic vascular resistance. Generic scheduled-cesarean ERAC regimens are not lesion-specific and should not be treated as cardiac guidance.
Avoid assuming a single hemorrhage or transfusion plan. Have blood products available when clinical risk warrants, including therapeutic anticoagulation or anticipated significant bleeding.

sections.title: Lesion-specific postpartum surveillance
bullets: Specify the monitoring location, rhythm surveillance, fluid balance, heart-failure warning signs and anticoagulation restart plan before delivery; update for actual obstetric and cardiac events.

Do not apply a fixed ICU duration to all cardiac conditions. Pulmonary arterial hypertension is an important exception to casual low-acuity recovery: ESC recommends intensive-care monitoring during and after delivery because postpartum risk is particularly high.

Other congenital, valvular or myocardial disease requires surveillance proportionate to severity, arrhythmias, ventricular function and the delivery course. Anticipate postpartum congestion and coordinate breastfeeding and medication planning with the specialist team.

sections.title: Obstetric airway rescue & extubation planning
bullets: Before GA, agree on aspiration risk, anticipated airway difficulty, positioning, preoxygenation, skilled help and a failed-intubation plan. Maintain uterine displacement when applicable and use head-up/ramped positioning when suitable.

Prioritize oxygenation. The OAA/DAS obstetric algorithm supports gentle mask ventilation after induction, limits repeated intubation attempts, and advises reducing or releasing cricoid pressure if it impedes ventilation or intubation.

After failed intubation, declare the problem and use facemask or an appropriate second-generation supraglottic airway for oxygenation. Decide whether to wake or proceed based on airway security, aspiration risk, maternal/fetal urgency and surgical needs.

A cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate emergency requires immediate escalation to emergency front-of-neck access under the trained local pathway; repeated unsuccessful instrumentation must not delay rescue.

Plan extubation and reintubation contingencies. Awake responsiveness, satisfactory ventilation/oxygenation and adequate neuromuscular recovery are prerequisites when applicable; airway edema, traumatic intubation, pulmonary edema or ongoing instability may justify continued ventilation and ICU care rather than forced extubation.

sections.title: Lesion-specific delivery & anesthesia distinctions
bullets: Use a documented Pregnancy Heart Team plan for significant disease, including lesion severity, ventricular/RV function, anticoagulation, delivery approach, rescue capability and postpartum surveillance. The 2025 ESC guideline uses the updated mWHO 2.0 framework.

Mitral stenosis: avoid treating this as a generic low-SVR lesion; tachycardia and congestion are important concerns. ESC prefers vaginal delivery in many patients but identifies severe stenosis or refractory heart failure as reasons to favor cesarean. Monitor closely after delivery for decompensation.
Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis: preserve perfusion and avoid abrupt hemodynamic changes; cesarean may be considered. Do not extrapolate this approach to an uncomplicated regurgitant lesion.

HCM with severe LVOTO: abrupt peripheral vasodilation is poorly tolerated. Use neuraxial techniques cautiously with a deliberate hemodynamic plan; severe LVOTO may favor cesarean, whereas lower-risk disease often permits vaginal delivery.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension/Eisenmenger: involve a PH expert, protect RV function and avoid sudden systemic vasodilation. ESC usually favors regional over GA and calls for intensive-care monitoring during and after delivery in PAH; this is not an ICU rule for all cardiac diagnoses.
Eisenmenger physiology also requires meticulous avoidance of air embolism; ESC recommends IV line filters. Balance bleeding and thrombosis risks individually.

Cardiomyopathy/arrhythmic disease: plan hemodynamic and rhythm surveillance, analgesia and volume management around the actual ventricular function and arrhythmia burden, including the postpartum period.

Mechanical valves: coordinate a written anticoagulation interruption/bridging and restart plan with cardiology, obstetrics and anesthesia. Do not independently stop VKA or apply a routine LMWH rule without considering valve-thrombosis risk; neuraxial eligibility must meet the applicable anticoagulant guidance.

sections.title: Uterotonics: cardiac lesion & hemorrhage context
bullets: Agree the hemorrhage and uterotonic plan before delivery. The 2025 ESC guideline generally favors oxytocin first-line, including higher-risk cardiac disease, but the agent, administration rate and hemodynamic response still require lesion-specific assessment.

The cardiac-anesthesia review advises titrating oxytocin by infusion pump because a rapid bolus can reduce SVR. Avoid replacing this with a generic scheduled-cesarean regimen when abrupt vasodilation is poorly tolerated.

Carboprost can increase pulmonary vascular resistance and provoke bronchospasm; the anesthesia review describes relative contraindications in pulmonary hypertension, right-heart compromise and preexisting asthma. A broad second-line listing in a guideline is not blanket clearance for these patients.

Methylergonovine can raise SVR and blood pressure and cause coronary vasospasm; the anesthesia review describes relative contraindications in hypertension, preeclampsia, aneurysms and coronary disease. Coordinate alternatives and hemorrhage escalation rather than treating it as interchangeable with oxytocin.

Misoprostol is among ESC’s second-line options in high-risk cardiac disease, but no uterotonic is a substitute for prompt recognition and control of hemorrhage. Specialist review should reconcile the regimen with the specific lesion and local obstetric pathway.

sections.title: Lesion-specific delivery & anesthesia distinctions
bullets: Use a documented Pregnancy Heart Team plan for significant disease, including lesion severity, ventricular/RV function, anticoagulation, delivery approach, rescue capability and postpartum surveillance. The 2025 ESC guideline uses the updated mWHO 2.0 framework.

Mitral stenosis: avoid treating this as a generic low-SVR lesion; tachycardia and congestion are important concerns. ESC prefers vaginal delivery in many patients but identifies severe stenosis or refractory heart failure as reasons to favor cesarean. Monitor closely after delivery for decompensation.
Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis: preserve perfusion and avoid abrupt hemodynamic changes; cesarean may be considered. Do not extrapolate this approach to an uncomplicated regurgitant lesion.

HCM with severe LVOTO: abrupt peripheral vasodilation is poorly tolerated. Use neuraxial techniques cautiously with a deliberate hemodynamic plan; severe LVOTO may favor cesarean, whereas lower-risk disease often permits vaginal delivery.

Pulmonary arterial hypertension/Eisenmenger: involve a PH expert, protect RV function and avoid sudden systemic vasodilation. ESC usually favors regional over GA and calls for intensive-care monitoring during and after delivery in PAH; this is not an ICU rule for all cardiac diagnoses.
Eisenmenger physiology also requires meticulous avoidance of air embolism; ESC recommends IV line filters. Balance bleeding and thrombosis risks individually.

Cardiomyopathy/arrhythmic disease: plan hemodynamic and rhythm surveillance, analgesia and volume management around the actual ventricular function and arrhythmia burden, including the postpartum period.

Mechanical valves: coordinate a written anticoagulation interruption/bridging and restart plan with cardiology, obstetrics and anesthesia. Do not independently stop VKA or apply a routine LMWH rule without considering valve-thrombosis risk; neuraxial eligibility must meet the applicable anticoagulant guidance.

bullets: Blood flow is a major determinant of extracorporeal oxygen delivery; sweep gas primarily controls CO2 removal. Overall oxygenation also depends on hemoglobin, native cardiac output, recirculation and metabolic demand.
Avoid abrupt large reductions in PaCO2 at initiation. Titrate support with serial gases and physiologic assessment.

Recirculation returns oxygenated blood directly to the drainage limb and reduces effective delivery. Worsening saturation despite increased pump flow should prompt assessment, not endless flow escalation.

sections.title: Peripheral VA: differential oxygenation
bullets: When recovering native cardiac output ejects poorly oxygenated pulmonary venous blood, the upper body may remain hypoxemic despite apparently good lower-body oxygenation.

bullets: Assess pulse pressure, aortic-valve opening, LV size/stasis and pulmonary edema. VA flow can increase afterload and impair LV ejection.

sections.title: Distal limb perfusion & vascular injury
bullets: Femoral arterial cannulation can compromise distal flow. Plan distal perfusion and serial clinical/Doppler or NIRS assessment according to configuration and local protocol.

sections.title: Anticoagulation, bleeding & thrombosis
bullets: Use the ECMO service’s anticoagulation strategy and serial coagulation/platelet/fibrinogen assessment. CPB ACT targets are not transferable to ECMO.

Do not equate ACT, aPTT and anti-Xa or escalate heparin from one discordant result alone. A 2025 VV-ECMO review describes inflammation/factor effects on aPTT and hemolysis, bilirubin or lipemia interference with chromogenic assays; review assay method and clinical context with the ECMO team/laboratory.

Interpret anticoagulation alongside bleeding, platelets/fibrinogen, circuit thrombus, circuit performance and patient perfusion. No single assay predicts every bleeding or thrombotic complication; direct-thrombin-inhibitor monitoring has additional assay limitations.

The review is VV-focused and is not a universal VA-ECMO target table. Anticoagulation interruption and resumption during bleeding or decannulation remain ECMO-service decisions with explicit circuit/patient thrombosis surveillance.

bullets: The 2026 gynecologic oncology ERAS table recommends holding daily GLP-1 therapy on the procedure day and weekly therapy for one week, with resumption on postoperative day one. This differs from the ASA-endorsed multisociety approach allowing continuation for most low-risk patients.

sections.title: VTE prevention & postoperative recovery
bullets: Assess cancer, prior VTE, obesity, immobility and bleeding risk. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with surgical hemostasis, renal function, drug interactions and neuraxial placement/removal; surgery timing does not override anticoagulant safety intervals.

For cancer laparotomy, the 2026 ERAS update recommends combined mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis and 28-day postoperative prophylaxis with LMWH or an appropriate DOAC. Drug choice requires an individualized bleeding, renal-function, interaction and adherence assessment; this is not a universal drug or dose prescription.

Do not automatically extend that 28-day regimen to minimally invasive surgery or minor benign procedures. The 2026 guideline favors mechanical prophylaxis for MIS and considers pharmacologic prophylaxis for high-risk patients, including a high Caprini score; follow the applicable oncology risk assessment.

The ERAS recommendation to initiate surgical prophylaxis preoperatively within two hours of incision is not permission to give LMWH immediately before neuraxial placement. ASRA recommends at least 12 hours after low-dose LMWH before needle placement; higher-dose regimens and renal impairment need their own assessment.

For twice-daily low-dose postoperative LMWH, ASRA requires the first dose the following day and at least 12 hours after needle/catheter placement, catheter removal before LMWH begins, and at least four hours from removal to LMWH. Use the full guideline for other regimens, traumatic placement and concurrent anticoagulants.

Support mobilization and oral nutrition within 24 hours when clinically appropriate. The ERAS regular-diet recommendation includes bowel resection, but instability, ileus, aspiration risk or specific reconstruction concerns require individualized surgical review, particularly after extensive exenteration.

sections.title: GLP-1 therapy: reconcile differing guidance
bullets: The 2026 gynecologic oncology ERAS table recommends holding daily GLP-1 therapy on the procedure day and weekly therapy for one week, with resumption on postoperative day one. This differs from the ASA-endorsed multisociety approach allowing continuation for most low-risk patients.

Do not translate either statement into an automatic patient instruction. Agree on a plan with anesthesia, the prescriber and surgery, considering dose escalation, gastrointestinal symptoms, other causes of delayed emptying, glycemic effects and the current institutional pathway.

For higher-risk patients the multisociety approach includes a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, adjustment of the anesthesia plan, and gastric ultrasound when appropriate expertise is available. Persistent concern may require delay of elective surgery; a medication hold or standard fasting interval does not prove an empty stomach.
Postoperative resumption also requires assessment of oral intake, nausea/vomiting, gastrointestinal function and the prescribing plan rather than an unconditional postoperative-day-one restart.

During active hemorrhage activate the local pathway early, follow perfusion and serial laboratory trends, and address hypothermia, hypocalcemia, fibrinogen/platelet deficits and coagulopathy as indicated.

A normal initial hemoglobin does not exclude acute major blood loss. Resuscitation and definitive surgical control proceed together; vasopressors may support perfusion but do not replace blood or correction of the bleeding source.

sections.title: Urinary tract injury & voiding plan
bullets: Clarify ureter/bladder dissection, cystoscopy and any repair with the surgeon. Unexpected hematuria, low drainage or abdominal findings need evaluation in context; urine output alone neither proves nor excludes urinary tract injury.

Document catheter duration and a voiding-trial/rescue catheter plan. Favor early removal when appropriate, but bladder repair, ureteric reconstruction or retention can justify longer drainage; avoid applying routine early-removal milestones to every complex pelvic operation.

sections.title: Major resection: organ support & handoff
bullets: Before extubation reassess ongoing blood loss, lactate/acid-base trajectory, temperature, coagulation, oxygenation and vasoactive needs. Persistent shock, major edema or respiratory failure may warrant continued ventilation and ICU rather than a routine immediate extubation goal.

Handoff blood products, fluid balance, drains/stomas, urinary reconstruction, electrolyte trends and analgesia/anticoagulant plans. Nutrition and mobilization should progress with the surgical recovery plan, not at the expense of managing evolving bleeding, sepsis or organ dysfunction.

sections.title: Team briefing & long-case protection
bullets: Before induction, confirm resection/reconstruction phases, anticipated blood loss, vascular access, blood products, analgesia and ICU availability. Arterial monitoring and large-bore access are often appropriate; central access is chosen for actual infusion/monitoring needs.

Reassess limb perfusion and pressure protection during prolonged lithotomy, allowing position changes when surgically feasible. Long duration, hypotension and compression compound compartment risk; maintain warming and reassess coagulation, electrolytes and acid-base status.

sections.title: Fluid accounting during urinary reconstruction
bullets: Urine output may be difficult to interpret or measure during urinary diversion/reconstruction. Integrate surgical losses, perfusion, blood gases and available dynamic/hemodynamic information rather than chasing a single urine-output target.

Use individualized fluid and vasoactive management; the PelvEx consensus does not establish one universal fixed-volume or inotrope regimen. Coordinate regional analgesia with bleeding risk, anticoagulation, hemodynamics and the planned postoperative neurological assessment.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & optimization
bullets: Confirm indication, approach, pregnancy possibility and testing with consent under local policy. Review anemia, bleeding history, anticoagulants, obesity/OSA, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal function, prior pelvic operations and baseline neurologic symptoms.

Investigate and treat iron-deficiency anemia and nutritional deficits before elective major surgery when time permits. Urgent hemorrhage or source control should not wait for completion of an elective optimization pathway.

For elective gynecologic oncology surgery, identify and treat the cause of preoperative anemia, including iron deficiency. The 2026 ERAS update supports preoperative optimization; the route of iron replacement depends on severity and time available rather than a universal regimen.

Apply a procedure- and aspiration-risk-specific fasting plan. The ERAS oncology pathway permits clear fluids until two hours before anesthesia and supports preoperative carbohydrate drinks; this is not clearance for a patient with obstruction, delayed gastric emptying, active vomiting or emergency surgery. Carbohydrate loading in well-controlled type 2 diabetes is a cautious, weak recommendation, not a routine instruction for all diabetes.

sections.title: Anesthetic technique & aspiration assessment
bullets: Choose local anesthesia with or without sedation, neuraxial anesthesia or GA according to procedure, duration, patient preference and rescue needs. MAC is an anesthesia service, not a fixed depth; sedation can progress to apnea and requires airway-rescue capability.

Assess vomiting, pain/opioids, reflux, obstruction, fasting and gestational stage individually. Early pregnancy alone does not establish delayed gastric emptying or mandate identical full-stomach management for every patient; active vomiting, shock or an emergency may still justify a protected-airway/rapid-sequence strategy.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & thermal care
bullets: Use appropriate ECG, blood pressure, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring; exhaled CO₂ is expected during moderate/deep sedation unless precluded or invalidated. Monitor temperature when clinically significant changes are intended, anticipated or suspected.

Match venous access, arterial monitoring and blood availability to hemorrhage risk and physiologic reserve, not the procedure name alone. Warm patients and substantial fluid/blood infusions; reassess hemoglobin, electrolytes, glucose and acid-base status as indicated.

sections.title: Lithotomy, pressure points & nerve protection
bullets: Document mobility limits and neuropathy; lift and lower legs together with adequate personnel. Protect the fibular head, heels and calves, avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction or external rotation, and avoid traction/compression on the brachial plexus or tucked arms.

Minimize time in lithotomy and steep Trendelenburg, reassess supports and perfusion when feasible, and avoid prolonged hypotension or concentrated calf pressure. Severe postoperative leg pain, swelling or weakness can signal compartment syndrome even with palpable pulses; obtain urgent assessment rather than attributing it automatically to a block.

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & fluid balance
bullets: Target euvolemia with reassessment of perfusion and measured losses; avoid both indiscriminate crystalloid loading and rigid restriction during bleeding. Distinguish vasodilation from hypovolemia or low cardiac output before choosing fluid, blood or vasoactive support.

Account for poor intake, bowel preparation, ascites drainage and irrigation absorption when relevant. Oliguria during pneumoperitoneum or pelvic manipulation is not by itself a mandate for repeated fluid boluses; inspect the catheter, hemodynamics and surgical context.

The 2026 ERAS guideline supports goal-directed fluid therapy for major gynecologic oncology surgery. Use an individualized hemodynamic assessment; it does not establish one universal monitor, fluid volume or vasoactive algorithm.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV prevention
bullets: Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with acetaminophen and an NSAID when renal function, bleeding risk and other contraindications permit. Local infiltration or an appropriate regional block may reduce incisional pain; blocks do not reliably eliminate visceral pelvic pain.

Assess PONV risk and use multimodal prophylaxis from different drug classes when indicated; consider propofol-based anesthesia and opioid reduction. Choose rescue antiemetics from a different class where possible and account for QT risk, sedation, urinary retention and other patient-specific effects.

For gynecologic oncology surgery, the 2026 ERAS recommendation is multimodal PONV prophylaxis with more than two antiemetic agents. Choose different classes with attention to contraindications and adverse effects rather than copying a fixed drug combination to every gynecologic procedure.

The updated oncology pathway supports multimodal analgesia, incisional local anesthetic or selected fascial-plane blocks, and intrathecal analgesia when appropriate. It does not make epidural analgesia mandatory; consider surgical extent, hemodynamics, anticoagulation, renal function and local expertise.

sections.title: Emergence, airway safety & disposition
bullets: Before extubation, confirm consciousness, airway protection, gas exchange, temperature and hemodynamic stability. After neuromuscular blockade verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; prolonged Trendelenburg also requires assessment for airway edema and a safe reintubation plan.

Arrange observation or higher-acuity care for persistent shock, major bleeding, airway swelling or respiratory compromise. Discharge requires controlled pain/nausea, appropriate bleeding assessment and procedure-specific voiding/catheter and return-precaution plans.

sections.title: VTE prevention & postoperative recovery
bullets: Assess cancer, prior VTE, obesity, immobility and bleeding risk. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with surgical hemostasis, renal function, drug interactions and neuraxial placement/removal; surgery timing does not override anticoagulant safety intervals.

For cancer laparotomy, the 2026 ERAS update recommends combined mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis and 28-day postoperative prophylaxis with LMWH or an appropriate DOAC. Drug choice requires an individualized bleeding, renal-function, interaction and adherence assessment; this is not a universal drug or dose prescription.

Do not automatically extend that 28-day regimen to minimally invasive surgery or minor benign procedures. The 2026 guideline favors mechanical prophylaxis for MIS and considers pharmacologic prophylaxis for high-risk patients, including a high Caprini score; follow the applicable oncology risk assessment.

The ERAS recommendation to initiate surgical prophylaxis preoperatively within two hours of incision is not permission to give LMWH immediately before neuraxial placement. ASRA recommends at least 12 hours after low-dose LMWH before needle placement; higher-dose regimens and renal impairment need their own assessment.

For twice-daily low-dose postoperative LMWH, ASRA requires the first dose the following day and at least 12 hours after needle/catheter placement, catheter removal before LMWH begins, and at least four hours from removal to LMWH. Use the full guideline for other regimens, traumatic placement and concurrent anticoagulants.

Support mobilization and oral nutrition within 24 hours when clinically appropriate. The ERAS regular-diet recommendation includes bowel resection, but instability, ileus, aspiration risk or specific reconstruction concerns require individualized surgical review, particularly after extensive exenteration.

sections.title: GLP-1 therapy: reconcile differing guidance
bullets: The 2026 gynecologic oncology ERAS table recommends holding daily GLP-1 therapy on the procedure day and weekly therapy for one week, with resumption on postoperative day one. This differs from the ASA-endorsed multisociety approach allowing continuation for most low-risk patients.

Do not translate either statement into an automatic patient instruction. Agree on a plan with anesthesia, the prescriber and surgery, considering dose escalation, gastrointestinal symptoms, other causes of delayed emptying, glycemic effects and the current institutional pathway.

For higher-risk patients the multisociety approach includes a liquid-only diet for 24 hours, adjustment of the anesthesia plan, and gastric ultrasound when appropriate expertise is available. Persistent concern may require delay of elective surgery; a medication hold or standard fasting interval does not prove an empty stomach.
Postoperative resumption also requires assessment of oral intake, nausea/vomiting, gastrointestinal function and the prescribing plan rather than an unconditional postoperative-day-one restart.

sections.title: Evidence scope & review boundary
bullets: Adult clinical-review draft, not an individualized anesthetic plan or independently approved protocol. Older positioning consensus and case reports support specified safety principles, not a newly validated universal protocol; current institutional guidance takes precedence for operational thresholds and rescue.

The anesthesia-facing ERAS content was reconciled against the 2026 full text on October 8, 2026. Oncology recommendations are scoped to the relevant operation; the GLP-1 guidance difference and independent clinical review remain explicit. This is not specialist approval or a complete institutional ERAS order set.
